items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: there was a Village Voice, Nat Hentoff had a memoir.

ctx.x: No. Actually I never thought about it until Duke Ellington died. Before that, you know it was just a Japanese traditional concept, or being Japanese playing jazz was some sort of a handicap. When I was growing up in Japan as a player, they always said that Filipino people have better feeling than Japanese, and indeed the Filipino players played better than us, and it’s simply because they have a longer history. They weren’t under — they were colonized by America so they are more exposed for jazz, much longer than…

So that has been going on for a long time. When Duke Ellington died, it was ’73, or ’74 I think, and there was a Village Voice, Nat Hentoff had a memoir. And he was talking about that fact that Duke was, how proud he was about his race. And he was pointing out so many music was based on his race, which I knew some…

However people always say that, you know I barely played for about thirteen years, and the people always say well you had a terrible time, a difficult time. And I never thought I am having a difficult time. Because everybody else did I thought. When I look back I think those times were very important times. items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Nat Hentoff had written sort of a memoir or memories of Duke in, I think it was Village Voice, and uh, when I read that and it….

ctx.x: It was like following him, so to speak, like that. And uh, Nat Hentoff had written sort of a memoir or memories of Duke in, I think it was Village Voice, and uh, when I read that and it…. You know, sometimes the little things have to be triggers and he was talking about how Duke was, how proud Duke was of being a black American, and his music [was] based on his race, a lot of „em, you know: “Black Butterfly,” what have you, “Black and Beige [Tan] Fantasy,” so on, blah, blah, blah. And even [if] you know it, still…

so when I read it I said, “Well, I‟m a jazz player; I‟ve been playing since I was sixteen years old, and so on, blah, blah. I‟m not a bad player, I have probably more experience than a lot of young American players, but I have a different heritage.” And uh, “I look at my heritage as my asset rather than my handicap, and maybe I can bring something into jazz tradition,” which it was, Japanese culture never was part of that. Maybe I could try to infuse something; maybe that would be my job. So, that‟s what…
